extracted.intended_audience: readers of political theory, historians, policymakers, and citizens concerned with democratic institutions
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and assess institutional and social signs by which democratic societies drift toward centralized, paternalistic power and the particular form of despotism that may arise. The subtask focuses on structural, administrative, economic, judicial, religious, and associative indicators that governments expand their prerogatives in democratic contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Love of equality as a condition of centralization
rubrics_metrics.description: The foremost or sole condition required to succeed in centralizing the supreme power in a democratic community is to love equality, or to get men to believe you love it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equality predisposes citizens to accept centralized power; revolutions aimed at equality often strengthen central authority. The text emphasizes that appealing to or embodying equality simplifies the 'science of despotism' to a single principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentration of sovereign attributes in the State
rubrics_metrics.description: The State resumes to itself natural attributes of sovereign power formerly exercised by private persons and corporations (administering justice, raising troops, levying taxes, making/interpreting law).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect when formerly intermediate/local authorities are eliminated and the State tolerates no agent between itself and the people; centralization of these sovereign functions is a clear marker of expanding government power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Erosion and disappearance of secondary/local authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Privileges of the nobility, liberties of cities, and powers of provincial bodies are destroyed or falling into dependence; local authorities are disappearing or becoming dependent on the sovereign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether local bodies' jurisdictions and autonomy are being narrowed or absorbed into central institutions; loss of municipal or provincial independence signals centralizing trends.

rubrics_metrics.name: State takeover of charitable, welfare, and educational functions
rubrics_metrics.description: The State undertakes to supply bread to the hungry, assistance and shelter to the sick, work to the idle, and acts as the sole reliever of misery; education and charity become national concerns with the State often taking children from mothers and training hearts/minds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for transfer of welfare, charity, and education from private or corporate hands to state administration, and for uniformity replacing diversity in public instruction; these shifts increase dependence and state reach into private life.

rubrics_metrics.name: State influence and control over religion
rubrics_metrics.description: Religion is in danger of falling into the hands of the government: rulers deprive clergy of property, pay them by salaries, and make them their own ministers or servants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicators include state provision/salary of clergy, reduction of clerical independence, and increased use of religious influence by the State to reach citizens' inner beliefs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inquisitive and minute administration (state interference in private life)
rubrics_metrics.description: Public administration becomes more inquisitive and minute, interfering in private concerns more than before, regulating more and smaller undertakings and advising or coercing private persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure expansion of regulatory reach into everyday private affairs, and proliferation of rules and inspections affecting small-scale activities as a sign of creeping administrative control.

rubrics_metrics.name: State centralization of capital and financial dependence
rubrics_metrics.description: The State centralizes large amounts of capital via loans from the wealthy and by absorbing the small savings of the poor (savings banks), so the nation's wealth flows around and through the government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor the State's role as debtor/creditor, its control or administration of savings institutions, and whether citizens' savings and loans increasingly pass through state mechanisms, creating economic dependence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improved, more efficient administration facilitating control
rubrics_metrics.description: Governments have improved the science of administration: they do more things with more order, celerity, and less expense, hold subordinate officers under stricter control, and invent new methods for guiding and inspecting agents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Efficiency and professionalization of administration can enable greater central power; track centralization of administrative agencies and tighter hierarchical control of agents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrowing independence of traditional judiciary and growth of state-controlled special courts
rubrics_metrics.description: Independent courts retain limited jurisdiction (private interests) while new dependent special courts arise to decide matters between government and private persons, subjecting the State's actions to less external sanction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for creation of administrative courts under government influence, reduced jurisdiction of ordinary courts over state disputes, and selection/control of judges by the State as erosion of judicial checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industrial/manufacturing growth as a cause of greater state power
rubrics_metrics.description: The growth of manufactures, fostered by equality, creates concentrated populations and complex relations requiring regulation and public works, thereby promoting increased government powers and interventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In contexts of industrialization, look for heightened regulatory regimes, state provision or control of infrastructure (roads, canals, harbors), and justification for state intervention on grounds of public necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: State ownership and regulation of strategic natural resources (mines)
rubrics_metrics.description: Governments assert rights of owning soil where mines lie, inspect and direct mining works, oust refractory operators, and transfer contracts—thus converting private mining property into state-controlled operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicators include legal claims of state ownership over mineral resources, extensive regulation of extraction methods, and governmental displacement of private operators.

rubrics_metrics.name: State as principal manufacturer and controller of production
rubrics_metrics.description: As State consumption of manufactured produce grows, the ruler becomes the principal manufacturer, collecting engineers and artisans in service to the government and tending to be the master of private manufacturers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the extent to which governments produce goods (arsenals, state factories), employ large numbers of producers, and exert control over private industrial combinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control and supervision of associations and combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Associations (combinations) are often required to be authorized by the State (inspection of by-laws), and the State seeks to place associations under its own control or superintendence, reducing their independence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for legal authorization regimes, state vetting of association rules, and regulatory frameworks that turn associations into dependent entities rather than independent civil society actors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public fear/jealousy of independent associations aiding state takeover
rubrics_metrics.description: Among democratic peoples, the populace may fear or distrust independent associations, considering their power dangerous and thus acquiesce in state regulation, which facilitates the State's absorption of associative power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy environments where citizens support restrictions on associations or welcome state oversight are susceptible to associative control by government; measure public attitudes and legal constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paternal, mild, extensive despotism that infantilizes citizens
rubrics_metrics.description: A new form of despotism: 'an immense and tutelary power' that is absolute, minute, regular, provident, and mild — like a parent that secures gratifications and keeps citizens in perpetual childhood, rendering free agency less useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify regimes that provide security and material comforts while simultaneously constricting civic initiative, private responsibility, and public thought; such regimes may not be violent but are deeply controlling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revolutions weakening old powers yet strengthening central authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Revolutions that overthrow aristocratic or ancient authorities to install equality often end up consolidating and extending the prerogatives of central power rather than dispersing it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating political change, consider whether dismantling traditional powers is accompanied by checks and balances or primarily results in concentration of authority at the center.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instinctive centralization despite political instability
rubrics_metrics.description: Even in periods of mutability, rapid changes in rulers and diverse interests, there exists an 'instinctive centralization' where many actors—wars, revolutions, policies—converge to increase central power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume political turbulence prevents centralization; instead, monitor administrative and institutional reforms that persistently draw power toward central structures regardless of regime stability.
